questions.q: What is Project 2's real value, according to this lesson's wrap-up?
options: Showing that big-bang cutover is always the right choice
Inventing brand-new modeling techniques not covered earlier in the track
Replacing the need for a retrospective
Proving that individually-taught techniques (grain, MERGE, freshness SLAs) compose into something a real migration actually needs
questions.explain: None of Project 2's pieces were new material — the project's value was proving they work together on one real system.

questions.q: Which earlier concept did the target warehouse's incremental load logic draw on?
options: The Lambda architecture's dual codepaths
A brand-new load technique invented specifically for this capstone
Big-bang cutover exclusively
The MERGE INTO pattern from Databricks & Delta Lake, applying source changes without a full table rewrite
questions.explain: The incremental load logic leaned directly on the MERGE INTO pattern taught in the Databricks & Delta Lake course.

questions.q: Why is a retrospective that only lists what went well considered insufficient?
options: It takes too long to write down what went well
It's a highlight reel, not a retrospective — the useful version specifically answers what worked, what you'd change, and what surprised you
Retrospectives are only useful for failed projects
A retrospective should never mention anything positive
questions.explain: A real retrospective answers all three questions specifically and in writing, while the details are still fresh.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the retrospective should be written the same day the project closes?
options: Because retrospectives expire after 24 hours
Because the outline requires it to be dated correctly
Because the client requires same-day documentation
Because memory of "what we'd do differently" fades fast, and specificity is what makes the retrospective useful later
questions.explain: Waiting loses the specific details that separate a real retrospective from a vague afterthought.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect the retrospective to a future job interview?
options: The retrospective should be hidden from interviewers
Interviewers only ask about what went well, never about changes
Retrospectives are never useful outside of the project itself
"What would you change?" is almost word for word the question an interviewer asks about any project on a resume
questions.explain: Having a real, specific answer ready — instead of inventing one under pressure — is the whole point of writing it down now.
